newsitem.title: USA: Netanyahu gets boost from U.S. Congress chairmen.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu gets boost from U.S. Congress chairmen.

text.p: In an implied rebuke to President Bill Clinton, the chairmen of the Senate and House of Representatives foreign affairs committees have assured Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of their support for Israel's security.

"There are voices who insist that it is incumbent upon the State of Israel to make all the sacrifices for peace. Do not count us among such people," Sen. Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican and Representative Benjamin Gilman, a New York Republican, wrote in a letter to Netanyahu dated on Tuesday.

The letter followed Clinton's comment on Monday that Israel's settlements policy had become an obstacle in talks with the Palestinians on Israel's planned troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron.

Israeli-Palestinian tensions have flared over Israel's decision to grant financial benefits to Jewish settlers in the West Bank, the killing of two settlers by Arab gunmen and the fatal shooting of an Arab by a Jewish farmer.
Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Gilman, who heads the House International Relations Committee, are both known for their strong support of the Jewish state.
Their letter said there had been "some excited discussion" in the United States about Israel's commitment to the Middle East peace process.

It called Israel a political, strategic and moral ally of the United States and a constant and trusted friend, adding: "These facts are immutable and cannot be altered by changes in government, either in Washington or Jerusalem."
The two chairmen said all parties to peace had to act in good faith, and peace would not hold or fail on the actions of one party alone.
"We would not presume to advise you on specific steps to take, or refrain from taking, in your pursuit of a just and lasting peace," Helms and Gilman wrote.

"We do, however, support your efforts to ensure the security of Israel's people and its borders. Security is the foundation on which the peace process has been built, and without which neither Israel, nor the United States, can be confident of a lasting solution to the conflict in the Middle East."

Meanwhile State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns urged the Palestinian Authority to reciprocate some of Israel's gestures in negotiations for redeployment of Israeli troops from the West Bank town of Hebron.

"In return for some of the gestures that have been made by the Israeli government in these negotiations just recently, we think the Palestinian Authority should now put itself in a position to reciprocate some of those gestures on the specific issues that are in play in these Hebron talks," Burns said.

The two sides renewed talks on Monday. Hebron is the last of seven West Bank towns from which Israeli troops are supposed to redeploy under previous accords, but the talks are bogged down over security arrangements for Hebron's 400 Jews.
